opus-5.5.text:
I think robotics is a field where the boundaries between components are much blurrier than people expect. If you only work on, say, the learning algorithm, and you treat the hardware, the data collection, the controllers, and the evaluation setup as black boxes someone else hands you, you end up missing where the real problems are. A lot of the time, when a policy fails, the reason isn't the model architecture at all. It's a calibration issue, a latency problem in the control loop, a camera that shifted, or data that was collected inconsistently. If you can't trace a failure through the whole stack, you can't really diagnose it, and you can end up spending months optimizing the wrong thing.

There's also a research-taste side to it. The most interesting questions often live at the interfaces, like how the way you collect data should shape the way you design the learning algorithm, or how the action representation interacts with the low-level controller. You only start to see those questions if you've gotten your hands dirty across the whole pipeline. Some of the ideas I'm proudest of came from noticing friction in a part of the system that wasn't supposed to be "my part."

And practically, it makes students much more independent. In a lab, if every project depends on handoffs between five people, everything moves at the pace of the slowest link. If a student can set up the robot, write the data pipeline, train the model, and run the experiments themselves, they can iterate fast, and iteration speed is really what drives progress in robot learning right now. It also prepares them for whatever comes after, whether that's starting their own lab, joining a company, or founding a startup. In all of those settings, being able to own a system end to end is incredibly valuable.

That doesn't mean everyone has to be the world's best at everything. People still develop deep expertise in one area. But I want them to have enough fluency across the stack that they understand how their piece fits into the whole, and they aren't afraid to open up any part of the system when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says students should be able to own a system end to end and understand how their piece fits into the whole, beyond working only on their assigned part.

r002.rationale: The response encourages fluency across the stack, but it does not state that no lab task is beneath any member.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I feel pretty strongly about, and part of it comes from my own experience. When I was a PhD student, the projects I learned the most from were the ones where I had to touch everything: the data collection, the learning algorithm, the robot infrastructure, the evaluation, even the demo video at the end. And the projects I learned the least from were the ones where I was handed a piece and told, "just make this module work."

In robotics especially, the parts are not really separable. If you're the person working on the policy learning side but you've never actually teleoperated the robot or looked at the raw camera streams, you'll make assumptions about the data that are just wrong. You'll think the failure is in the model when it's really a calibration issue, or latency in the controller, or a gripper that slips under certain loads. And conversely, if you only do hardware and controls, you don't develop the intuition for what a learning system actually needs from the data. The interesting problems in robot learning live at the boundaries between these layers, and you can't see those boundaries if you only stand on one side.

There's also a more practical reason. Research moves fast, and the thing you're specializing in today might be commoditized in two years. What doesn't go away is the ability to look at a whole system, figure out where the real bottleneck is, and go fix it, whatever layer it lives in. That's the skill I want my students to leave with. I'd rather they be slightly slower on a given project because they're learning the full pipeline than be very fast at one piece and helpless when that piece isn't the problem.

And honestly, it makes the lab healthier. When everyone understands the full stack, people can actually help each other debug, cover for each other when someone's traveling or on an internship, and have real conversations about the research direction instead of just reporting status on their component. Ownership of a whole problem, end to end, is also just more motivating. It's your project, not your subroutine.

I will say it's not that I want everyone to be equally good at everything. People should still go deep somewhere. But "full-stack" to me means you're never blocked by a part of the system you're afraid to open up. You should be able to read it, modify it, and reason about how it interacts with your piece. That's the bar.

r001.rationale: The response says students should take ownership of a whole problem end to end and understand the full project pipeline, beyond one component.

r002.rationale: The response encourages students to engage with every system layer, but does not state that no lab task is beneath any member.

astra-6.text:
Because I want students to develop ownership of the whole problem. If you only work on one piece of a project, it’s easy to take the inputs, the assumptions, and even the goal as given. But when you have to make the whole system work, you start asking: Are we solving the right problem? Is the bottleneck really the algorithm, or is it the data, or something in the system?

That doesn’t mean everybody needs to be an expert in everything. You can still have a specialty and collaborate with people who have complementary strengths. But understanding how the pieces connect helps you make better decisions within your own specialty, too.

Ultimately, I want students to be able to take an idea and carry it through—to build it, test it, understand why it fails, and decide what to try next. That independence is a big part of becoming a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response says students should develop ownership of the whole problem and be able to carry an idea through the full process, beyond their individual piece.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether any lab task is beneath a lab member.

sol-6.1.text:
I want students to understand how their piece fits into the whole system. If you’re working on one part of a robotics project, the assumptions you make affect everything downstream. And when something doesn’t work on the robot, you need to be able to figure out whether the problem is in the model, the data, the perception system, or the control.

That doesn’t mean everyone has to be an expert in everything. You can still have a specialty. But having experience across the stack helps you ask better research questions, collaborate with other people, and take an idea all the way to something that actually works. That independence is what I want students to develop.

r001.rationale: The response says students should understand how their work fits the system and be able to carry an idea through to implementation, but it does not clearly say they should take responsibility for the lab project as a whole beyond their own contributions.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that no lab task is beneath any member.
